phonemes.desc: Rough breathing on upsilon with acute [hýp], the pitch peak of the name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HOOP-nohs' — the first syllable is pitched high and begins with a rough 'h'; the second is short and level.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: Possible root *(s)up- 'to sleep'; cognate with Latin sopor and English 'sleep'

kin.label: Twin
kin.form: Θάνατος (Thánatos), his twin brother, the personification of death

pronunciation.note: Hýpnos is Tier 2 because the Greek Ὕπνος preserves the acute stress on the first syllable but has no long vowel. He and his twin Thánatos are children of Night (Nyx) and live near the sunset.

domains.title: The Tender-Eyed God
domains.subtitle: Sleep, Dreams, Release
domains.lead: Hýpnos is the personification of sleep, the gentle twin of death who brings rest to gods and mortals. He moves through the world on silent wings, touching tired eyelids with a branch or a whisper.

cards.name: Personified Sleep
cards.desc: One of the children of Nyx; sleep comes to all equally, slave and king.

cards.name: Wings of Quiet
cards.desc: Often shown with wings at his temples or heels, swift and soundless.

cards.name: Dream-Giver
cards.desc: He opens the gates through which Oneiroi, dream-spirits, pass to sleeping mortals.

cards.name: Brother of Death
cards.desc: Thanatos and Hypnos together carry the dead from the battlefield.

symbols.name: Poppy
symbols.meaning: The soporific flower associated with sleep and dreams

symbols.name: Wings at the temples
symbols.meaning: The swift arrival of sleep and its power to lift the soul into dream

symbols.name: Branch or horn
symbols.meaning: The wand with which he sprinkles sleep upon the eyes

symbols.name: Dark mist
symbols.meaning: The shadowy garment in which he wraps the sleeper

mythology.lead: Hýpnos is a minor but indispensable power. Gods call on him when they need a mortal or immortal to fall unconscious, and poets love him as the brother who daily rescues humanity from wakefulness.

myths.title: Hera Bribes Hypnos
myths.text: In Iliad 14, Hera asks Hypnos to lull Zeus to sleep so she can aid the Greeks. Hypnos recalls an earlier occasion when Zeus had hurled him from heaven in anger and demands a guarantee. Hera promises him Pasithea, one of the Graces, and he agrees. He pours sleep over Zeus's eyes while the god embraces Hera on Mount Ida.

myths.title: Sleep and Death Carry Sarpedon
myths.text: When Zeus's son Sarpedon is killed by Patroklos, he instructs Apollo to have Hypnos and Thanatos carry the body to Lycia for burial. The twins lift the hero gently, 'swift as thought,' and bear him away. The scene is one of the Iliad's tenderest images of death.

myths.title: Son of Night
myths.text: Hesiod makes Hypnos a child of Nyx, born without a father alongside Thanatos, the Keres, and other dark powers. He dwells in a cave near the land of the Cimmerians, where the sun never enters, and from there he moves across sea and land to bring rest.

lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Hypnos with Somnus, whose mythology largely mirrors the Greek. In later antiquity he was associated with Morpheus, the dream-shaper, and with the Cimmerian cave as a portal to the underworld. Christian writers demonized pagan sleep-deities but retained the poppy and the winged image in depictions of Death. Modern psychology has reclaimed Hypnos through the term 'hypnosis,' though the connection is more romantic than clinical.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hýpnos lives in the word 'hypnosis' and in every lullaby, sleeping pill, and bedtime ritual. He is the god of the third of life we spend unconscious, the realm where memory, fear, and desire recombine. In art he appears as a beautiful winged youth, sleep's beauty made visible. His twinship with Thanatos reminds us that every sleep is a small rehearsal for death.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Hýpnos is the god who visits everyone. Rich and poor, hero and coward, all close their eyes at his touch. In this he is more democratic than any Olympian. Yet he is also dangerous: sleep can be bribery, escape, or the doorway to deception, as when Hera uses him against Zeus.

The Greeks did not trust sleep entirely. Dreams could be true or false, divine or merely digestive. Hypnos therefore carries ambivalence: he restores and he disables, he heals and he makes vulnerable. To honor him is to acknowledge our daily surrender of consciousness — the small death without which no waking is possible.
lore.archaeology: Hypnos was represented in Greek and Roman art as a winged youth, often at the bedside of the dying or carrying a hero's body. The famous bronze head of Hypnos from the British Museum, found in Civitella d'Arna, shows the god with wings at his temples. Votive and funerary art frequently pairs him with Thanatos.
